title: Chapter 1: Your First Program and Your AI Study Partner
video_title: Python Chapter 1: Your First Program and Your AI Study Partner
summary: Install Python, write and run your first program, control output with print, sep and end, and read your first error messages. You will also set up an AI assistant as a tutor, with three safety habits, and catch an AI mistake that runs without an error.

beats.narration: Welcome to Code Quest, Chapter 1: Your First Program and Your AI Study Partner. Today you will write and run your first Python program, and you will learn to use an AI assistant as a tutor.

beats.narration: First, a puzzle. A learner asked an AI assistant to print today's date as 2026, hyphen, 11, hyphen, 09, using three separate values. The AI wrote this line of code.
The code runs without an error. But does it do what the learner asked?
Here is the real output. There are spaces where the hyphens should be. Code that runs is not always code that is correct. By the end of this chapter, you will know why, and how to fix it.

scenes.title: Why this matters
scenes.direction: Three short ideas: programs are instructions, output shows what a program does, and you remain the checker.

beats.narration: Every app you use is a program. A program is a list of instructions that a computer follows exactly. Your phone's calculator, a shop's checkout screen and a train timetable all start as instructions like the ones you will write today.

visual.heading: Every app is a program
items: A **program** is a list of instructions that a computer follows exactly.
A calculator, a checkout screen and a train timetable all start as instructions.

beats.narration: Output is the first skill you need. When a program shows a message, you can see what it is doing. Professional developers often use print to check that their code works.

visual.heading: Output shows what a program is doing
items: When a program shows a message, you can see what it is doing.
Developers often use `print()` to check that their code works.

beats.narration: AI assistants such as ChatGPT and Claude can now write code. You still need to understand that code. AI tools are often right, but they can also be wrong while sounding confident. A study of AI tutors in Harvard's CS50 course found exactly this. You are the person who runs the code and decides if it is correct.

visual.heading: AI writes code. You check it.
items: AI assistants such as ChatGPT and Claude can write code.
They are often right, and sometimes wrong while sounding confident.
You run the code, check the result and decide if it is correct.

scenes.title: The idea: Python reads from top to bottom
scenes.direction: The diagram, then the definitions of function and string, then the recipe analogy with its limit.

beats.narration: A Python program is a text file that ends in dot p y. Each line is an instruction. Python, the program called the interpreter, reads your file and carries out each instruction in order: top to bottom, one line at a time.

visual.heading: How Python runs a program
body: The **interpreter** reads your `.py` file and carries out each line in order.
visual.pre:
You write          Python reads          The computer acts
 +-----------+      +--------------+      +-------------------+
 | hello.py  | ---> |  line 1      | ---> | shows line 1      |
 | (text)    |      |  line 2      |      | shows line 2      |
 +-----------+      +--------------+      +-------------------+
                     top to bottom,
                     one line at a time

beats.narration: Print is a function: a named action that Python already knows. You call it by writing its name, then brackets. The value inside the brackets is what it shows. Text must be inside quotation marks, and text in quotation marks is called a string.

visual.heading: Two words you need
items: A **function** is a named action Python already knows. Call it with its name and brackets: `print(...)`.
A **string** is text inside quotation marks: `"Hello"`.

beats.narration: Think of a program like a recipe. The cook follows each step in order and does exactly what it says. The comparison stops at one point. A cook can guess what you meant, but Python cannot. If a step has a typing mistake, Python stops and reports an error.

visual.heading: A program is like a recipe
items: The cook follows each step in order, exactly as written.
Where it stops working: a cook can guess what you meant. Python cannot.
A typing mistake makes Python stop and report an error.

beats.narration: Step 1: install Python. Check the official guide for your system on python dot org. The current version is Python 3.15, and any version from 3.12 works for this course. On Windows, install the Python install manager from python dot org or the Microsoft Store.

Usually installed already; otherwise use your package manager

beats.narration: On macOS, download the installer package from python dot org and open it. On Linux, Python is usually installed already. Then open a terminal and check the version. You should see a line that starts with Python 3.

beats.narration: Step 2: create your first file. Open a code editor, such as Visual Studio Code, or IDLE. Create a file called ex 0 1 hello, and type these lines. Line 1 starts with a hash sign, so it is a comment. Python ignores comments. They are notes for people.

visual.heading: Step 2: Create your first file
visual.hidden_text: Run it to see the output.

beats.narration: Step 3: run the file. In the terminal, go to the folder that holds your file. Type python, then the file name, on Windows. Type python3, then the file name, on macOS and Linux.
You will see two lines. Each print produces one line of output. The quotation marks do not appear, because they only mark where the text starts and ends.

scenes.title: Step 4: Check the order
scenes.direction: Predict before the reveal. Then challenge the learner to swap two lines.

beats.narration: Step 4: check the order. This program prints three steps for making tea. Predict the output before you run it.
In which order will the lines appear?

visual.question: In which order will the three steps appear?

beats.narration: The lines appear in the same order as the code. Now swap two lines in your file and run it again. The output changes, because Python always runs from top to bottom.

scenes.title: Step 5: Several values, sep and end
scenes.direction: Explain the two settings with a table, show the code, pause on lines 4 and 5, then reveal.

beats.narration: Step 5: print several values at once. Print can take more than one value, separated by commas. It also has two settings. Sep sets what goes between the values, and its default is one space. End sets what goes after the last value, and its default is a new line.

visual.heading: Step 5: Two settings of `print()`
rows: What goes after the last value

beats.narration: Look at this program. Line 2 adds 3 and 4 without quotation marks. Line 3 sets sep to a hyphen. Line 4 sets end to three dots.

visual.heading: Step 5: Several values, sep and end

beats.narration: Predict the output, especially lines 4 and 5.

visual.question: What do lines 4 and 5 print together?

beats.narration: Line 2 has no quotation marks around 3 plus 4, so Python calculates it and prints 7. Line 3 joins the values with a hyphen instead of a space. Line 4 ends with three dots instead of a new line, so line 5 continues on the same line: Loading, dot dot dot, done.

visual.heading: Step 5: Several values, sep and end

scenes.title: Work with AI: a tutor, not a machine
scenes.direction: Safety habits, the six stages, two prompt cards, then the AI pair moment from the opening.

beats.narration: Use an AI assistant as a tutor that explains, not as a machine that does your work. Follow three safety habits from today. One: never paste passwords, keys or private information into an AI tool. Two: run every piece of AI code yourself, and compare the output with what you asked for. Three: you are responsible for the code you use, even if an AI wrote it.

visual.heading: Three safety habits
items: Never paste passwords, keys or private information into an AI tool.
Run every piece of AI code yourself and compare the output with what you asked for.
You are responsible for the code you use, even if an AI wrote it.

beats.narration: AI helps at every stage. Plan the steps in plain English. Write the program yourself first, then ask for an explanation. Generate code from an exact output. Debug with the full error message. Test by comparing outputs. And improve with at most two suggestions.

visual.heading: AI at every stage
columns: How to use AI in this chapter
rows: Ask for the steps of a welcome card in plain English, with no code yet.
Write it yourself first. Then ask AI to explain each line.
Paste the exact output and ask for code that uses only `print()`.
Paste the code and the full error. Ask for the cause before the fix.
Ask AI to compare expected and real output, space by space.
Ask for at most two readability suggestions, each with a reason.

beats.narration: Here is the Write card. Paste your code, and ask the AI not to rewrite it. Ask it to explain each line in one simple sentence, and to say whether it prints exactly the output you want. Then run your program. If the AI said yes but the output differs, trust the real output.

visual.heading: Prompt card: explain, do not rewrite
visual.label: Write
visual.prompt: Here is my Python code: <paste your code>. Do not rewrite it. Explain what each line does in one simple sentence, and tell me if it prints exactly this: <paste the output you want>.
visual.check: Run your program. If the AI said yes but the output differs, trust the real output.

beats.narration: And here is the Generate card. Paste the exact output you want, and ask for code that uses only print. Then compare every character, including spaces. This is how the date flaw was caught.

visual.heading: Prompt card: code for an exact output
visual.label: Generate
visual.prompt: Write Python code that uses only the print() function. It must output exactly these lines, with the same spaces and symbols: <paste the exact output>. Show the code, then show the output it produces.
visual.check: Run the code and compare every character, including spaces, with your target.

beats.narration: Now the AI pair moment. Back to the opening puzzle. The request asked for hyphens, but the output has spaces. Which setting did the AI forget?

visual.heading: AI pair moment: find the flaw

beats.narration: Think about step 5.

visual.question: Which setting puts a space between the values? How do you change it?

beats.narration: The AI forgot that sep is a space by default. The fix sets sep to a hyphen, and the date prints correctly. Always check AI output against what you asked for, character by character.

visual.heading: The fix: set `sep` to a hyphen

scenes.title: Common mistakes
scenes.direction: One beat per mistake with the real error, then the reading habit.

beats.narration: Now, four common mistakes. Mistake 1 is a missing closing quotation mark. Python cannot see where the text ends, so it reports a Syntax Error. A syntax error means Python could not read the file, so no line runs. The fix is to add the closing quotation mark before the bracket.

visual.heading: Mistake 1: a missing closing quotation mark

beats.narration: Mistake 2 is a capital letter in print. Python treats capital P Print and small p print as different names. Notice that Start was printed first. This error happened while the program was running, so the lines before it had already run. The message names line 3, and even suggests the fix.

Mistake 3 is curly quotation marks. Word processors and some chat apps change straight quotation marks into curly ones. Python only accepts straight ones. Type the quotation marks again in your code editor, and copy code from a code block, never from a formatted document.
Mistake 4 is a missing closing bracket. Every opening bracket needs a closing bracket.
The habit to build: read the last line of an error first. It names the kind of error. Then look at the line number to find where it happened.

beats.narration: Let's recap. A program is a list of instructions, and Python runs them one at a time, from top to bottom. Print shows values. Text goes inside quotation marks, and calculations without quotation marks are worked out first.

items: A program is a list of instructions. Python runs them from top to bottom.
`print()` shows values. Text goes in quotation marks; calculations are worked out first.
`sep` controls what goes between values, and `end` what goes after them.
An error names the kind of error and the line. Read the last line first.
AI is a tutor. Ask it to explain, then run and check everything yourself.
